e.t: This Greek LXX verb means “ripen.” It describes something becoming mature or fully developed, especially as a person, child, or living thing reaches a later stage of growth. The word occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical corpus, so its basic idea is consistent even though the surrounding subjects may differ. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is said to be ripening and the surrounding context.

This adjective describes someone or something as “not-working; idle”—inactive rather than engaged in useful labor. It can characterize a person who is unwilling or unable to work, or a condition marked by inactivity. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Proverbs, so its basic sense is connected with the contrast between productive effort and idleness. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis falls on a person’s behavior or on the inactive condition itself.

This Greek LXX adjective means “not offered.” It describes something that has not been presented as an offering. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, at Leviticus 19:7. Its basic sense is limited and straightforward: it identifies something as not offered, while the surrounding verse determines what object or offering is being described. The word itself does not express a broader spiritual lesson apart from that basic description.

This noun means “uncleanness,” referring to a condition of impurity or defilement. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used especially in passages concerned with conditions that made a person, object, place, or community unclean before God. Its meaning is therefore broader than ordinary dirtiness: it describes a state requiring recognition and, where Scripture specifies it, cleansing or separation. The word occurs 52 times in the Greek Old Testament, including the deuterocanonical books, with many occurrences in Leviticus and Ezekiel.

This word means “elsewhere” or “in another place.” It is an adverb that points away from the place or situation currently being discussed, directing attention to a different location. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, once in Wisdom and once in 2 Maccabees. Its basic function is straightforward: it identifies another place rather than the present one. The surrounding verse determines exactly which place is intended in each occurrence.

Amaria is a personal name used for people in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies individuals rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears twelve times across ten verses, especially in genealogical and family lists in 1 Chronicles and Nehemiah. It also appears in Deuteronomy and Ezra. Its precise significance belongs to the name itself; the available wording establishes Amaria as a proper name without giving an additional lexical definition.

Aminadab is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament, also rendered Aminathav. It is not presented here as a common word describing an action, quality, or object, so its meaning is chiefly its use as a personal name. The name occurs 27 times in 25 Old Testament verses, appearing in genealogical and narrative settings across several books. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on which person named Aminadab is being mentioned.

This noun means “forgetting” or “forgetfulness”—the loss, absence, or failure of remembrance. It names a condition in which something is no longer remembered, rather than describing an action such as deliberately ignoring someone. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Sirach 11:25. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains the absence or loss of memory.

This noun means “bucket” or “ladle,” referring to a container or utensil used for lifting or carrying liquid. It names a practical object rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Chronicles 4:16. The exact role of the object in that passage depends on the surrounding verse text, but its basic meaning remains a bucket or ladle. These two meanings describe the same general kind of implement: something used to scoop, hold, or transfer material.

This verb means “impress again”: to press, stamp, or mark something anew. It describes a repeated act of making an impression rather than a first marking. As a verb, it expresses an action performed on something or someone, but the available lexical meaning does not identify the exact object or purpose here. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Wisdom 14:17; the surrounding verse is needed to explain its particular force there.

This adverb means “unexpectedly,” describing something that happens in a way a person did not anticipate. It focuses on the surprising manner or timing of an event rather than naming the event itself. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Wisdom 11:7. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains clear: something takes place contrary to what was expected.

“Worthily” is an adverb describing an action as being done in a worthy manner. It tells how something is carried out, rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, this word occurs three times, all in the deuterocanonical books of Wisdom and Sirach. Its basic meaning remains concise: an action is performed worthily. The precise force in any one passage depends on the sentence and surrounding context.

This verb means to “delude” or “deceive”—to lead someone away from the truth or a right understanding. It can describe misleading another person, whether through false impressions, misleading words, or deceptive influence. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 40 times, showing that this is a recurring word for deceptive action rather than a rare expression. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding context.

This word means “simply,” expressing something done or stated in a straightforward, uncomplicated way. It is an adverb, so it describes how an action occurs or how a statement is presented rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. In this Greek LXX corpus, it appears three times across Proverbs, Wisdom, and 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding words, but its central idea remains directness and simplicity.

This word is a proper name rendered “Arabi” or “Aravi.” It identifies a person by name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs two times, both in Nehemiah. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word itself functions as a personal name. The two recorded occurrences are Nehemiah 2:19 and Nehemiah 6:1.

Rapacious describes someone marked by greedy, aggressive taking—eager to seize what belongs to others rather than acting with restraint. It is an adjective, so it characterizes a person or creature by this predatory quality. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, at Genesis 49:27. Its precise force in that verse depends on surrounding context, but its central meaning is greedy, aggressive taking.

Asas is a proper name, referring to someone called “Asas.” It functions as a name rather than as a description, command, or action. In the Greek Septuagint corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 2 Chronicles 20:16. The available lexical information identifies the name but does not provide the verse text or enough surrounding context to explain more about the individual.

Asor is a proper name identifying someone or something called Asor. It is rendered simply as “Asor,” so no broader ordinary meaning is supplied for this word. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Joshua 19:37. The reference identifies where the name appears, but without the verse text, its specific referent cannot be explained further here. Its meaning is therefore best understood as the name Asor itself, rather than as a descriptive word or action.

This word means “transgression”: a violation or departure from what is commanded or right. It functions as a noun or adjective, identifying wrongdoing or something marked by such wrongdoing. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all in four verses: three in Ezra and one in Jeremiah. Its basic sense remains focused on transgression itself, while the surrounding passage determines the particular matter being described.

Achire, also rendered Akhire, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an idea, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears six times, with five occurrences in Numbers and one in 1 Kings. The name is associated with individual biblical references, but the available information does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain the person’s role or significance. Its meaning here is therefore its identity as the personal name Achire or Akhire.

This noun means “torment”: intense suffering or distress, especially the painful experience imposed on someone. It names the suffering itself rather than describing an action or person. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, which are not included here. The word’s central idea remains severe anguish or painful affliction.

Beria is a proper name, rendered as “Beria” or “Veria.” In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. This name occurs twice in the LXX, both times in 1 Chronicles 23:10–11. The name itself supplies identification, while the surrounding verse and passage are needed to determine the person’s precise role in those genealogical records.

This noun means “north wind,” referring to wind coming from the northern direction. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for a directional wind rather than for a person, place, or abstract idea. The word appears 150 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including passages in Genesis, Numbers, Joshua, Psalms, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on how the surrounding passage describes the wind’s movement or effect.

This word is a proper name, referring to “Gaba” or “Gava.” It is not a general term describing an action, quality, or object, but a name used in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs once in the LXX, in Nehemiah 11:31. Since the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s specific role in that passage cannot be explained further; its basic meaning is the named entity itself.

This noun refers to a trap or cage used to hold an animal, specifically a weasel trap or a cage for beasts. Its basic meaning is a physical enclosure designed to catch or confine, rather than a person or an abstract condition. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Ezekiel 19:9. The English rendering there is cage, which fits the word’s stated sense.

Galilōth is a proper name, rendered “Galilōth” or “Galiloth.” As a name, it identifies a particular named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 18:17. The available wording does not provide a broader definition beyond the name itself, so its precise referent is determined by the surrounding passage rather than by an abstract meaning of the word.

This Greek LXX noun means “laughter,” referring to laughter as an expression or sound. It can describe the presence of laughter without, by itself, specifying whether the occasion is joyful, mocking, foolish, or sorrowful; the surrounding passage supplies that nuance. The word occurs 20 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, showing a recurring term for laughter across these writings. Its basic meaning remains simple and consistent: laughter itself. [p03:word:lxx:L703032:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L703032:occurrences]

This verb means “carve”: to cut or shape material into a form. It describes an intentional act of making something by working on its surface or substance. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 12 times, including passages concerning skilled work connected with sacred furnishings and building. The word focuses on the work being done—forming something through carving—rather than on the finished object itself. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what material or object the surrounding passage identifies.

This LXX word refers to a secretary or the work associated with a secretary. It is a verb, so it presents secretary-related activity rather than simply naming a person. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in 1 Chronicles 26:29 and once in Jeremiah 52:25. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine its precise force in either passage.

Dalal is a proper name, also given as “Thalal.” It identifies a named person or place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This Greek LXX name appears once in the corpus, at Joshua 15:38. Because no verse text or surrounding context is available here, its specific referent cannot be described further; the supported lexical information establishes the name itself and its alternate rendering.

“Bite” or “sting” means a painful injury inflicted by teeth or by a stinging creature. It is a noun describing the resulting wound or painful effect, rather than the action itself. This word occurs three times in the LXX corpus, in Micah and Wisdom, and its usage remains concrete and physical. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun means an order: an authoritative instruction, ruling, or decree issued for others to follow. It refers to something formally declared rather than a casual request or personal suggestion. The word appears three times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, in Ezra, Esther, and Wisdom. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and situation, but its central idea remains a binding or authoritative command. It does not itself describe whether the order is wise, just, or obeyed.

This noun refers to deliberation or release. It can name careful consideration when a matter is weighed, or the act of letting something go. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Wisdom 12:20, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic sense remains centered on either thoughtful consideration or release, rather than describing a person, object, or action more specifically.

Dōthaim is a proper name for a place, also rendered “Thothem.” It does not describe an action, quality, or spiritual concept; it identifies a location in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs three times in two verses, in Genesis and 2 Kings. Because the available information identifies the name but does not provide the surrounding verse text, its particular significance in either passage must be understood from the wider context of those passages.

This adjective describes something that is “inscribed; written”—put into written form. It refers to a written record or words set down in writing. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, at Psalm 149:9. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its precise force in that sentence cannot be explained further, but its basic meaning remains something written or inscribed.

This Greek adjective describes something selected or regarded as choice—something distinguished from what is ordinary or less preferred. It can describe people or things that are specially chosen, valued, or excellent. The central meaning is “select; choice.” In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 94 times, so its precise force depends on the noun or subject it describes. It appears across books such as Genesis, Psalms, Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Jeremiah.

Ellanathan is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing a general idea, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 24:8. The available lexical information preserves the name as “Ellanathan,” without an additional ordinary-language definition or English rendering. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person identified there.

This LXX verb means “let,” expressing permission or allowance. It describes allowing something to take place rather than preventing it. The word occurs twice in the LXX corpus, once in Psalms and once in 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on what is being allowed and the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains permission: giving room for an action or event to occur.

This Greek LXX adjective means “900,” expressing the quantity nine hundred. It describes a number connected with something being counted, such as years, people, or other items, depending on the sentence. The word occurs 15 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, from Genesis through Nehemiah. Its meaning remains specific and numerical rather than carrying a broader abstract idea. The surrounding words determine what is being numbered, while this word itself supplies the value nine hundred.

It means to hang in the sun. As a verb, it describes the act of leaving something or someone suspended in sunlight. The word appears three times in the Greek Old Testament, all within 2 Samuel 21, at verses 6, 9, and 13. Its central meaning is physical and concrete: hanging in direct exposure to the sun, rather than simply being in sunlight or experiencing heat.

This Greek LXX verb means “drive against” or “drive home”: it describes forceful action directed onto or against something. As a verb, it expresses doing rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Esther 5:1 and Proverbs 3:18. Those references show its limited distribution, but without the verse text they do not establish the precise force intended in either setting. Its central idea remains directing something forcefully against a target.

This word means “seventeen,” the number that comes after sixteen and before eighteen. It is an indeclinable number word, so it identifies a quantity rather than describing an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, each in a different verse: 2 Kings 13:1, 1 Chronicles 7:11, and 2 Chronicles 12:13. Its exact significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject being counted.

This Greek LXX adjective means “different” or “alternate.” It describes someone or something that is not the same as another, distinguishing one person, object, or choice from another. The word can therefore identify an additional person, a contrasting option, or something belonging to another category. It occurs 226 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so its exact nuance depends on the noun or situation it describes. Its basic sense remains comparison: one is other than, or different from, another.

gl: day old; kept till the morrow
d: day old; kept till the morrow

e.t: This adjective describes something that is a day old or has been kept until the next day. It points to age or storage across a short period, rather than something fresh from the same day. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Ezekiel 4:14. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning concerns something retained until the morrow.

Zabet, also rendered Zavet, is a personal name rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 11:41. Because the available information gives the name and its reference but not the surrounding verse text, its significance here is limited to identifying the person named Zabet or Zavet.

This word means “beer,” referring to a fermented drink. It is a noun, so it names the drink rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 19:10. That single occurrence establishes its ordinary lexical meaning, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain its particular significance there. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that translation’s language and corpus.

This verb means to gird—to fasten something around oneself, especially clothing or a belt. It describes the practical act of securing what is worn around the body. The word appears 15 times in this Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical corpus, showing a recurring action rather than a rare technical term. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This Greek LXX noun means “victim” or “offering”—something presented in sacrifice. It names the sacrificial object rather than the act of giving or the person who gives it. The word occurs ten times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including passages in Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, and later historical books. Its precise emphasis in any verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is a sacrificial offering presented to God.

Ianatha is a proper name, functioning as a specific designation rather than a general descriptive word. In the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, it appears once, at 2 Samuel 5:16. The lexical information preserves the name as “Ianatha” but provides no additional meaning or description. Therefore, readers should understand it as the name itself, while the surrounding verse and passage determine whom or what it identifies and what role it has there.

This Greek LXX noun means “priesthood” or “priest’s office,” referring to the role or service belonging to priests. It describes priestly responsibility rather than a person’s name or a specific act. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Samuel 2:36. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s precise force in that passage must be understood from its context, but its central meaning remains the priestly office or the condition of serving as a priest.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Iēsoue” or “Iisue.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs twice: once in 1 Chronicles 7:27 and once in Ezra 2:6. Because the available information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, it does not establish further details about the person or the significance of either occurrence. The name’s precise reference is therefore determined by each passage’s context.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Iōsabee” or “Iosavee.” It identifies a particular person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 11:2. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the name’s specific role in that passage cannot be described further. Its meaning is therefore best understood as the personal name itself.

“In that” is a conjunction or adverb that links one statement with another by pointing to the matter being referred to. It helps direct attention to a specific fact, circumstance, or point already in view. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs 57 times across 54 verses, so it is a recurring connective expression rather than a rare term. Its precise force in any passage depends on the surrounding sentence.

This noun means “badness; vice”: a morally wrong quality or corrupt behavior. It describes evil as a condition or practice rather than naming one particular sinful act. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this LXX corpus, it occurs 131 times, showing that the word is used broadly for moral wrongdoing. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains a settled pattern of badness or vice.

This word describes something “with edible fruit.” It is a noun referring to a fruit-bearing tree or plant whose fruit can be eaten. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Deuteronomy 20:20. The word’s central idea is usefulness as a source of food: its fruit is suitable for people to eat. The precise role it plays in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains focused on edible fruit rather than merely having fruit.

This verb means “oppress”: to deal harshly with people by placing them under heavy control or burden. It describes an action imposed on others rather than a feeling or condition. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, it occurs 10 times, showing a recurring description of cruel or burdensome treatment. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means “distribute” or “allot”: it describes giving something out or assigning portions to others. It presents an action of dividing and assigning what is available rather than merely possessing it. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 79:14. The precise force of the action in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, which is not included here, but the word itself centers on allocation or apportionment.

This Greek LXX verb means to “put into cantonments” or “encamp”—to arrange people, especially a group or army, in a settled camp or military station. It describes the act of establishing a camp rather than merely traveling or passing through a place. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, once in Joshua and once in 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and situation.

This noun means “piece,” referring to a portion or fragment of something rather than the whole. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used seven times across seven verses, including passages in Leviticus, Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, and Ezekiel. Its central idea remains simple: a distinct part separated from, taken from, or belonging to a larger whole. The surrounding verse determines what kind of piece is meant, but the word itself emphasizes the portion or fragment.

This noun means “conference,” referring to a gathering in which people come together for discussion or deliberation. It names the meeting itself rather than a person, action, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 14:22. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain the particular purpose or significance of that conference in its passage.

This proper name refers to the Kretes, also called Krites. It identifies a people rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, the word appears three times: twice in Ezekiel and once in Zephaniah. Its exact significance in any one passage comes from the surrounding verse and its wider context, but the basic meaning remains the name of this people. The word occurs in Ezekiel 25:16, Ezekiel 30:5, and Zephaniah 2:5.

This noun means “fringe” or “edge,” referring to a border or projecting outer part of something. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Exodus, where the wording concerns the edges or fringes of items. The core idea is a distinct outer boundary rather than the main body of an object. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding description, but the word consistently points to something situated at the margin or extremity.

This word means “cypress,” the name of a tree. It is a noun used for the tree itself rather than for an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it occurs 12 times, including passages in 2 Kings, Job, Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Sirach. Its repeated use as the name of a tree gives it a straightforward, concrete meaning; the significance of the tree in any particular verse depends on that verse’s surrounding context.

This noun means “tongs” or “snuffers,” naming a tool used to handle or tend something small and delicate. It refers to an instrument rather than an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, the word appears four times. It is rendered “snuffers” three times and “tongs” once, showing that both terms express its basic meaning. Its uses occur in Exodus, Numbers, 2 Chronicles, and Isaiah.

This noun refers to rock that is smooth and exposed, with no covering or soil hiding its surface. It can describe a bare rocky place or a rock made smooth. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs four times, all in Ezekiel. Its two closely related senses—“smooth rock” and “bare rock”—emphasize the visible, uncovered character of the rock rather than a particular shape or size. The surrounding verse determines which aspect is most prominent in a given occurrence.

Mabsan, also rendered Mavsan, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies one individual in the Greek Old Testament and occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 1:29. Because the available passage text is not included here, the name’s specific family connection or role cannot be explained from this lexical entry alone. Its meaning is therefore the identification of the person who bears the name, not a separate vocabulary concept.

“Far away” describes something at a distance, whether a person, place, or object is spatially removed. As an adverb, it tells where something is or how separated it is, rather than naming the thing itself. In the Septuagint, it occurs 67 times, showing a recurring expression for distance across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings. Its exact force—such as distance from a location or from someone—comes from the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains being far off or away.

This noun means “manna” or “gift.” It identifies something given, with “manna” pointing specifically to the provision known from Israel’s Scriptures. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, at Nehemiah 13:5. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the precise way the word functions in that passage must be understood from its context. Its basic meaning remains a gift or manna, referring to something received rather than produced by the recipient.

“Megala” is a proper name, functioning as the name of a specific person, place, or other named entity rather than as an ordinary descriptive word. The supplied lexical meaning is simply “Megala,” so its exact referent must be determined from the surrounding passage in each occurrence. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, this name occurs 43 times, beginning in Genesis and continuing through Sirach. The name itself does not provide enough information to identify its referent without the verse context.

Mestraim is a proper name, rendered “Mestraim” or “Mestrem.” It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament tradition rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 1:8. Since no verse text or surrounding passage is included here, the name’s specific family relationship or role in that genealogy cannot be stated from this word alone. Its basic meaning is therefore the personal name itself: Mestraim, also known as Mestrem.

This LXX particle means “surely” or “certainly.” It strengthens a statement by expressing firm assurance, making the speaker’s words sound definite rather than hesitant. As a particle, it modifies the force of a sentence instead of naming a person, thing, action, or quality. It occurs 316 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so it is a recurring way of emphasizing certainty across these writings. Its exact emphasis in any verse depends on the sentence surrounding it.

Misadai, also rendered Misathe, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a person or named individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, once at Leviticus 10:4 and once at Deuteronomy 10:6. Without the surrounding verse text, Scripture here does not provide a broader meaning for the name itself; its primary function is to designate someone by name.

This Greek LXX noun means “falling snow” or “snowstorm,” referring to snow as it descends or to a storm of snow. It names a natural weather event rather than an action, person, or spiritual quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in Deuteronomy 32:2 and Daniel 3:68. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its ordinary meaning remains the same: snow falling from the sky, especially when understood as a snowfall or snowstorm.

This adjective means “eighteenth,” identifying something that comes after the seventeenth in an ordered sequence. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for dates, reigns, appointments, or numbered divisions, depending on the surrounding sentence. It occurs 14 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including 13 occurrences in Old Testament books and one in a deuterocanonical book. Its precise reference—such as a year, day, or assigned group—must be determined from the verse’s surrounding text.

This noun means “hoof,” specifically a solid hoof. It refers to the hard covering at the end of an animal’s leg. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it is used especially when describing animals and the physical feature that helps identify them. The word occurs 18 times in this LXX corpus, with many occurrences in Leviticus and Deuteronomy, where animal characteristics are described. Its basic meaning remains concrete and straightforward: the hoof itself, rather than the whole animal or its leg.

e.h: A Greek LXX Word for Bake
e.t: This Greek LXX verb means “bake”: to cook food with heat, especially in an oven or other heated place. It describes an action rather than an object or person. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament translation, appearing from Genesis through Isaiah. Its uses concern preparing food, including bread or meat, and can also describe baking for personal use. The exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains the act of baking or cooking with heat.

This adjective describes someone as responsible and devout—faithful in conduct and committed to honoring what is right before God. It presents a person’s character rather than naming an action, object, or place. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, the word occurs 54 times, showing that this quality is a recurring concern, especially in Psalms, Proverbs, and Wisdom. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a life marked by responsible faithfulness and devotion.

This word means “craftiness”: clever, often deceptive skill used to achieve an aim. As a noun, it describes a quality or method rather than an action itself. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, it occurs eight times, appearing in passages concerned with people who use shrewdness or concealed purposes. The word can describe practical cleverness, but its setting may show whether that cleverness is wise or morally suspect. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

“Frenzy-stricken” is an adjective describing someone overtaken by frenzy. It presents a condition affecting a person, rather than naming an action or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, at Deuteronomy 28:34. The verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, so the precise force in that sentence depends on context, while the basic meaning remains “frenzy-stricken.”

This Greek LXX noun means “sitting beside,” describing someone or something positioned alongside another. Its basic idea is nearness in a place or position beside another, while the surrounding sentence determines the precise role. It occurs twice in the Greek text of Wisdom, in Wisdom 6:14 and Wisdom 9:4. The word’s central picture remains simple: one who or something that is present beside another rather than distant or separate.
